explain.say: Hang a chain between your hands and it takes a graceful curve. Flip that curve upside down and you have the shape of a perfect arch. Robert Hooke wrote about this in sixteen seventy five, and Gaudí designed churches with hanging chains. On the board, a cable hangs over a forty metre span and an arch rises above it.

explain.say: Here is the secret link. A forty metre beam carrying five kilonewtons per metre would have a peak moment of one thousand kilonewton metres. A cable carrying the same load takes up exactly the shape of that moment diagram, upside down, with no bending at all: it carries everything by pure tension.

explain.say: Never, the pull would have to be endless! The arch is the mirror image: the same two hundred and fifty kilonewtons, but as a push called thrust. Its feet shove outward and down on the abutments, the solid blocks at each end, and the ground must push back. Weak ground under an abutment and the arch spreads and falls.

faq.q: Why does a cable take a curved shape?
faq.a: A cable can only carry tension, so it hangs in whatever shape puts its loads into pure pull. Under a load spread evenly along the span that shape is a parabola, the upside-down moment diagram.
Thrust is the horizontal push an arch exerts on its supports. An arch carries load in compression, so its feet push outward, and the abutments must resist it.
asks: Why does an arch push outwards?

faq.q: How do you find the horizontal tension in a cable?
faq.a: Divide the simple-beam moment by the sag: H equals w L squared over 8 d. For 5 kilonewtons per metre over 40 metres with 4 metres sag, H is 250 kilonewtons.

faq.q: Why does a smaller sag mean a bigger tension?
faq.a: The moment the cable must balance is fixed by the load and span, and H times the sag must equal it. A smaller sag means a shorter lever arm, so H must grow.

faq.q: Why do arches need strong abutments?
faq.a: An arch only stands while its feet cannot spread. The abutments and ground must resist the outward thrust; if they move, the arch flattens and can collapse.

facts: Under a load spread evenly along the span, a cable hangs as a parabola with horizontal tension H = wL²/8d.
Robert Hooke published the hanging-chain principle for arches in 1675, hidden in a Latin anagram.
The Akashi Kaikyō Bridge in Japan has a main span of 1991 metres.
